findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Trading Company Update as at Quarter 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Council is contingently liable for 50% of £35m development partnership costs, with £9.2m committed and 2026-27 business plan approvals delayed.
findings.detail: Harrow Strategic Development Partnership is a 50/50 joint venture with Wates Construction covering Poets Corner, Peel Road, Byron Quarter and Grange Farm developments. Total HSDP expenditure to 30 June 2026 is £35.048m; of this £16.636m relates to Milton Road (funded separately by HRA). The Council's contingent 50% share of the remaining £18.412m is £9.206m. The paper explicitly states the Council is in effect underwriting 50% of any HSDP expenditure incurred. Wates has cashflowed pre-construction costs to date, but finance costs (interest on Wates loan) have accumulated to £3.458m. Critically, phase business plans for 2026-27 have not yet been approved, creating governance and visibility gaps.
findings.matters: The Council carries a material contingent liability in a £35m+ development partnership with undefined total scope, full exposure to future costs beyond the £9.2m already recorded, and delayed governance controls.
findings.figures: £35.048m total expenditure to June 2026; £18.412m non-HRA spend; £9.206m Council liability (50%); £3.458m finance costs accrued
findings.quote: As equal partner with Wates in this joint venture arrangement, the Council is responsible for 50% of any expenditure incurred within the HSDP, i.e. £9.206m being the liability up to June 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Trading Company Update as at Quarter 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Concilium Assets LLP income fell 34% short of budget in 2025-26 due to strategic shift from commercial rental to social housing for homeless families.
findings.detail: Concilium Assets LLP operates 53 PRS units acquired to generate commercial rental income. In 2025 the Council decided to repurpose units for longer-term housing for homeless families via Assured Periodic Tenancies instead of private rental sector lettings. Actual income in 2025-26 was £405,483 against a business plan budget of £613k—a shortfall of £208k. A net loss of £241k is budgeted for 2026-27 as a result of the PRSO implementation. The paper states the Council will benefit from cost reductions elsewhere in the budget for homelessness accommodation.
findings.matters: The Council has redirected an asset away from commercial returns toward social provision, creating a significant forecast miss (34%) and embedding planned losses going forward, raising questions about budget discipline and forecasting accuracy.
findings.figures: £405,483 actual vs £613k budget (2025-26); £208k shortfall; £241k loss budgeted (2026-27)
findings.quote: Council received a total of £405,483 in 2025/26 for both lease rent and dividend. This is lower than the budgeted sum of £613k in the business plan due to the transition from PRS activity to using the units for offering longer-term housing to homeless families.

findings.paper_title: report - CTS
findings.headline: Council cannot isolate scheme impact from economic factors after one year; retaining scheme pending 2027/28 review

Findings based on single financial year; collection rates are evaluated over three-year period. Council recommends retaining current scheme for 2027/28 and conducting further review then.

findings.paper_title: report - CTS
findings.headline: 72.8% of people who lost CTS eligibility in April 2025 remained up to date with Council Tax payments
findings.detail: 671 claimants lost CTS eligibility from 1 April 2025. Sample review of 10% found 72.8% were up to date with payments, with remainder at various enforcement stages. Of those sampled, 9 had moved homes and 51 were maintaining current payments despite loss of support.
findings.matters: Positive counterbalance to enforcement escalation. Shows scheme changes, while reducing support to a vulnerable group, did not trigger widespread non-payment in the cohort most directly affected.

findings.paper_title: report - CTS
findings.headline: Summonses to working-age CTS claimants jumped 66.9% to 1,667 in 2025/26, the year of benefit cuts
findings.detail: Working-age CTS claimants received 1,667 summonses in 2025/26, up from 999 in 2024/25. This 668-summons increase coincided with April 2025 scheme changes that reduced maximum awards to 50% for non-vulnerable claimants. Council attributes increase to combination of scheme impact and changes to enforcement parameters. Around 550 working-age CTS claimants receive summons each year persistently.
findings.matters: A cohort already on Council Tax Support (lower-income households) facing reduced support saw enforcement action escalate sharply. Persistent summons to ~550 people annually suggests entrenched collection difficulties in vulnerable population.
findings.figures: summonses to working-age CTS claimants: 993 (2023/24), 999 (2024/25), 1,667 (2025/26); increase of 668 year-on-year

findings.paper_title: report - CTS
findings.headline: In-year collection rate fell to 95.65% while council budget assumes 98% collection over three-year rolling period
findings.detail: 2025/26 in-year collection rate was 95.65%, down from 96.49% in 2024/25, reflecting national downward trend. Council's annual budget assumes 98% collection rate achieved within a three-year period, implying reliance on arrears collection to bridge the in-year gap. Council states this assumption has historically been met and projects it will be maintained.
findings.matters: If in-year collection rates continue to fall, the council's ability to maintain 98% three-year average depends on arrears collection. Timing mismatch creates cash-flow risk if arrears collection slows.
findings.quote: a 98% collection rate has consistently been assumed for that purpose based upon attaining that level within a three-year period and for which historically, that has generally been achieved. Based upon current and projected collection rates, that appears likely to be maintained for the future.

findings.paper_title: report - CTS
findings.headline: Council achieved £1.7m gross savings from April 2025 scheme changes but in-year collection rate fell to 95.65%
findings.detail: Scheme changes reducing maximum awards for working-age non-vulnerable claimants to 50% achieved intended £1.7m gross (£1.3m net of GLA share) savings. Council Tax Support expenditure fell from £19.1m (2024/25) to £18.3m (2025/26). However, in-year collection rate fell from 96.49% (2024/25) to 95.65% (2025/26), following national downward trend.
findings.matters: Savings targets that land on paper but drive collection difficulties signal a shift in collection risk. A lender needs to know if cost reduction was achieved by pushing payment pressure onto lower-income households.
findings.figures: £1.7m gross savings; £1.3M net; expenditure £19.1m → £18.3m; collection rate 96.49% → 95.65%
findings.quote: The changes proposed were determined to achieve £1.7m gross savings, equating to £1.3M once the GLA's share of the reduction was accounted for.

findings.paper_title: Acquisition and refurbishment of a property for young adults with a disability

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Housing Complaints Report
findings.headline: Overall complaint volume increased 33.5% (from 522 to 697 complaints) with Tenant Satisfaction Measure complaint rate per 1,000 homes rising from 89.82 to 127.71
findings.detail: Total Housing Ombudsman-jurisdiction complaints increased from 522 in 2024/25 to 697 in 2025/26 (+175, +33.5%). The Tenant Satisfaction Measure complaint rate per 1,000 properties rose from 89.82 to 127.71. Stage 1 complaints increased 18.8% (458 to 544). The council attributes the increase to 'a combination of factors, including increased resident awareness of the complaints process, improved identification and recording of complaints, greater compliance with the Housing Ombudsman's Complaint Handling Code and broader complaint definitions, and increased pressures on Landlord Services.' While improved recording may account for some increase, the concurrent rise in justified complaint rates (75.6%) suggests genuine increase in service failures rather than process change alone.
findings.matters: A 33.5% increase in complaints combined with 75.6% being justified indicates substantially increased service delivery problems in a major council function, not merely improved awareness. This suggests demand pressures that may require capital or revenue investment.
findings.figures: Total complaints: 522 (2024/25) to 697 (2025/26), increase of 175 or 33.5%; Stage 1 complaints: 458 to 544 (+18.8%); TSM complaint rate per 1,000 homes: 89.82 (2024/25) to 127.71 (2025/26)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Housing Complaints Report
findings.headline: One-quarter of complaints are repeats from the same household or property, indicating agreed remedies are not being delivered or underlying issues recur
findings.detail: At household level, 137 complaints (25.2% of 544 Stage 1 complaints) were repeats from the same household after excluding the first complaint. At property level, 120 complaints (22.1% of Stage 1) were repeats at the same property. The council acknowledges that repeat complaints 'may arise from recurring service failure, incomplete resolution, delays in completing agreed actions and separate issues raised by the same household' and has flagged this as requiring further analysis to identify 'whether repeat complaints arise from recurring service failure, incomplete resolution, delays in delivering agreed remedies, separate service issues or an ongoing property-related problem.' High repeat complaint rates indicate that case resolution is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Repeat complaints from one-quarter of complainants indicate that agreements are not being honoured, issues are recurring despite investigation, or the council lacks capacity to deliver agreed actions. This creates ongoing liability and undermines trust.
findings.figures: 25.2% of Stage 1 complaints were repeats at household level (137 of 544); 22.1% at property level (120 of 544); 87 households made more than one complaint; 78 properties had more than one complaint

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Housing Complaints Report
findings.headline: Stage 2 escalations nearly doubled (139.1% increase) and represent 28.1% of Stage 1 complaints, indicating complaints are not being resolved at first contact
findings.detail: Stage 2 complaints rose from 64 to 153 (+89 complaints, +139.1%), increasing from 14.0% to 28.1% of Stage 1 demand. Of these, 56 Stage 2 complaints were responded to late during 2025/26, compared with 34 in the previous year. The report notes that 'Stage 2 demand grew considerably faster than Stage 1 demand' and acknowledges further analysis is needed to determine whether escalation relates to 'the original service response, the Stage 1 investigation or remedy, delays in completing agreed actions, communication, or recurring and complex service issues.' This high escalation rate suggests systemic failure to resolve complaints at first contact.
findings.matters: High escalation rates indicate either that initial decisions are wrong or that underlying issues are not being resolved, both of which require additional council resources and prolong liability exposure.
findings.figures: Stage 2 complaints: 64 (2024/25) to 153 (2025/26), increase of 139.1%; Stage 2 as % of Stage 1: 14.0% to 28.1%; 56 Stage 2 responses late in 2025/26 vs 34 in 2024/25

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Housing Complaints Report
findings.headline: Resident satisfaction with complaint handling collapsed from 28.3% to 17.3% despite dramatic improvement in response timescales
findings.detail: While the council improved Stage 1 on-time responses from 57.0% to 79.6% and Stage 2 responses from 43.8% to 63.4%, satisfaction with complaint handling fell sharply from 28.3% in 2024/25 to 17.3% in 2025/26. The council acknowledges that 'compliance with complaint response timescales alone does not determine resident satisfaction. Rather, the quality of communication, and the ability to resolve underlying issues remain critical factors.' This indicates that faster processing is masking failures to actually resolve residents' problems.
findings.matters: Fast processing of bad decisions does not reduce liability or improve service delivery. Low satisfaction combined with high complaint volumes and high failure rates suggests the underlying service problems are unresolved and may worsen.
findings.figures: Tenant Satisfaction Measure TP09 (satisfaction with complaint handling): 28.3% (2024/25) to 17.3% (2025/26)

Within Housing and Regeneration, major schemes show substantial delays: Grange Farm Phase 2A (£13.460m slipped), Byron Quarter within HSDP (£10.356m slipped), HRA Property Acquisition (£13.989m slipped). The paper acknowledges 'delays across the Council's major regeneration schemes... where planning, commercial negotiations, design development, and stakeholder engagement necessarily extend delivery timelines'.
findings.matters: Low capital delivery rates and multi-year delays suggest project management challenges and may indicate risks to the viability of regeneration schemes. If housing development cannot be delivered on schedule, the council may not achieve expected capital receipts or housing supply targets, affecting both asset values and future revenue from completed schemes.
findings.figures: Capital budget: £226.070m; Outturn: £75.594m (33%); Slippage: £146.932m; HRA capital programme 27% delivered (£22.530m of £83.783m)
findings.quote: The level of rephasing reflects delays across the Council's major regeneration schemes, including sites within the Harrow Strategic Development Partnership (HSDP) and elements of the High Priority Planned Maintenance programme for corporate properties. These schemes are at early or preparatory stages, where planning, commercial negotiations, design development, and stakeholder engagement necessarily extend delivery timelines.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn - New Template v2
findings.headline: Children's services placement costs overspend £4.2m; UASC grant does not cover full cost
findings.detail: Placements overspend of £4.191m includes residential children's homes, residential parenting assessments, and supported accommodation. There is explicit 'budget pressure on UASC placements since Home Office grant income does not fully fund the cost of accommodation and support for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and young people'.
findings.matters: The council is bearing costs on top of Home Office grant for vulnerable young people. This is demand-led and driven by factors outside the council's control (asylum flows). It represents an unfunded mandate pressure.
findings.figures: Placements overspend: £4.191m; Total Children's Services overspend: £5.471m
findings.quote: Budget pressure on UASC placements since Home Office grant income does not fully fund the cost of accommodation and support for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and young people.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn - New Template v2
findings.headline: Parking charge notice income under-recovered by £2.4m; unachieved MTFS savings on EV charging
findings.detail: The Environment directorate reported a £2.437m pressure on Parking Services relating to 'an under-recovery of income from penalty charge notices (PCN) issued'. The paper also notes Highway Services experienced a cost pressure of £522k, which includes '£300k relates to unachieved MTFS savings (income from EV charging)'. This is material because the council was relying on these income sources to balance budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's income projections are reliable. The parking undershoot of £2.4m suggests either demand has fallen or the council cannot enforce at projected levels. The missed EV charging savings suggest forward-looking income plans are not materializing.
findings.figures: Parking PCN under-recovery: £2.437m; EV charging unachieved savings: £300k; Total Environment overspend: £2.980m
findings.quote: Parking Services: a net pressure of £2.437m, relating to an under-recovery of income from penalty charge notices (PCN) issued.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn - New Template v2
findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £4.4m driven by rising costs of complex needs; Mental Health service showing surge in demand
findings.detail: Adult purchasing overspend of £2.158m, with the paper noting the service 'has encountered increasing costs of care packages from clients with complex needs and requiring more expensive care', and that 'the current budget overspend predominately relates to the Mental Health Service, where the service has seen a rise in demand and costs throughout the financial year'. Children and Young Adults with Disability (CYAD) overspend of £3.582m from 'increased demand and rising costs from both existing and new care packages', with 'a significant proportion of the budget continues to be consumed by a relatively small number of high-cost complex cases'.
findings.matters: Both Adult Social Care and CYAD are showing uncontrolled demand-led growth on complex, high-cost cases. These are volatile, hard-to-predict spending areas. The council is managing them via agency staff and temporary measures, not structural solutions, which suggests costs will continue to rise.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care purchasing overspend: £2.158m; CYAD overspend: £3.582m; Total Adult & Public Health directorate overspend: £4.393m
findings.quote: The service has encountered increasing costs of care packages from clients with complex needs and requiring more expensive care, although the outturn position is in line with service projections from the start of the financial year. The current budget overspend predominately relates to the Mental Health Service, where the service has seen a rise in demand and costs throughout the financial year.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn - New Template v2
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has reached £28.7m and continues to grow despite government support for historic deficits
findings.detail: The DSG reserve stands at a cumulative deficit of £28.737m at 31 March 2026, up from £13.789m opening balance. The 2025/26 in-year overspend was £14.533m, predominantly from the High Needs Block (£16.887m). The government has confirmed it will fund up to 90% of accumulated deficits through a Section 31 grant, but this 'does not address the ongoing financial pressures arising from continued growth in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), increasing complexity of need, inflationary pressures and rising placement demand'.
findings.matters: Even with government support for historic deficits, the council faces unresolved structural pressures in High Needs that will continue to generate deficits in 2026/27 and beyond. This is not a one-off problem. The council acknowledges future support is 'linked to the delivery of local SEND reform plans and ongoing evidence of financial sustainability'—implying the council must demonstrate reform, not just access funding.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit: £28.737m; In-year 2025/26 overspend: £14.533m; High Needs Block overspend: £16.887m
findings.quote: The statutory override relating to Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) accounting arrangements has been extended until March 2028... any future support is expected to be linked to the delivery of local SEND reform plans and ongoing evidence of financial sustainability and system reform.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn - New Template v2
findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs spiralling with no funding solution: £13.8m annual subsidy loss and growing demand
findings.detail: Nightly paid accommodation placements grew from 497 to 645 households during the year. The council faces an annual subsidy loss of £13.8m because housing benefit subsidy rates have been frozen since 2011 while rental costs continue to inflate. The paper states this pressure is 'structural' and 'not expected to reverse in the short term', and explicitly describes it as 'one of the most material demand led risks facing the Council'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can sustainably fund this growing demand or whether it will continue consuming general reserves. The £13.8m gap is twice the council's total revenue underspend, making homelessness the single largest unresolved financial pressure.
findings.figures: Placements: 497 to 645; Annual subsidy loss: £13.8m; 2025/26 overspend on Housing General Fund: £2.572m
findings.quote: The overspend is predominantly structural, driven by sustained growth in demand for temporary accommodation and a long-standing mismatch between housing benefit subsidy and actual cost of provision.

findings.headline: MTFS budget gap of £22.2m persists across four-year plan with only £544k reduction
findings.detail: The Budget Planning Reserve for the MTFS gap shows £22.8m at 31/03/2025, reducing only to £22.2m by 31/03/2029. Over the full four-year medium-term strategy, only £544k of this structural gap is closed despite planned savings, suggesting planned reductions are either not landing or insufficient.
findings.matters: A persistent £22m structural gap after savings indicates revenue budget imbalance that cannot be resolved through planned efficiency and may require further reserve drawdown, service reductions, or borrowing.
findings.figures: Budget Planning Reserve MTFS gap 31/03/2025: £22,766,082; 31/03/2029: £22,222,082; net reduction: £544,000

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation reserve of £7m to be completely depleted by end of 2025/26
findings.detail: The Temporary Accommodation Demand Fund, standing at £7m on 31/03/2025, is forecast to be fully released (drawn down) by 31/03/2026 with no balance carried forward. This reserve was created to manage demand volatility in temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of a demand-smoothing reserve in a single year suggests either unsustainable temporary accommodation costs, demand higher than budgeted, or inadequate revenue provision. This creates risk of budget pressure if demand remains elevated in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Schools funding deficit growing to £68m by 2029, classified as unusable
findings.detail: The DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) overspend grows from £13.8m at 31/03/2025 to £32.1m by 31/03/2026 and reaches £68.1m by 31/03/2029. It is explicitly marked as an unusable reserve, meaning the council cannot deploy these funds to deliver services or offset other budget pressures.
findings.matters: A £68m unusable deficit represents a structural funding gap in schools that the council cannot resolve at budget level. DSG deficits accumulate annually and increasingly constrain councils' financial flexibility without relief from central government.

findings.paper_title: Final Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2028-29 v3 Cabinet briefing
findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising from 11.98% to 13.58% of net revenue budget in three years, with additional £3.559m in new scheme costs
findings.detail: Capital financing costs will increase from £33.784m (11.98% of £281.992m net revenue budget) in 2026/27 to £38.304m (13.58%) in 2028/29. New capital proposals add a further £3.559m in financing costs across the 3-year period. This shows capital financing costs consuming an increasing proportion of the council's net revenue budget, indicating rising leverage.
findings.matters: Rising capital financing costs as a proportion of revenue budget signal increasing leverage and reduce the council's flexibility to absorb shocks or fund other priorities.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £33.784m (11.98% of budget); 2028/29: £38.304m (13.58%); additional financing from new proposals: £3.559m
findings.quote: The capital financing cost of the Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2028/29 (to be agreed at Council in February 2026) is £33.784m in 2026/27 and then increases to £38.304m by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Final Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2028-29 v3 Cabinet briefing
findings.headline: £17.374m government school funding not yet profiled; £714k SEN unit funding pending dialogue
findings.detail: The government confirmed £17.374m alternative school funding but 'the funding profile is not made available yet.' The council will not include this in the capital programme until 'the 2026/27 allocation will be notified in Spring 2026.' Additionally, £714k for a proposed SEN unit remains outside the approved programme pending 'follow-up dialogues on this proposed cancellation with the Government.' Both items represent delayed and uncertain delivery.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed government funding timelines create risk of project delays and late-stage re-profiling, affecting planned school place delivery.
findings.figures: Alternative school funding not yet profiled: £17.374m; SEN unit funding outcome uncertain: £714k
findings.quote: Total alternative funding of £17.374m, to be profiled over 3 years, has been confirmed. However the funding profile is not made available yet. It is anticipated that the 2026/27 allocation will be notified in Spring 2026... For this reason, this budget is not yet included in the Final Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Final Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2028-29 v3 Cabinet briefing
findings.headline: Revenue savings from £28.952m of capital investment are assumed but not guaranteed
findings.detail: Three major programmes — Invest to Save (£15m), Property Acquisition Programme net borrowing (£10.452m), and In-House Residential Provision (£2.5m) — are funded entirely from borrowing with the expectation that capital financing costs will be offset by operational savings. The council explicitly states: 'the requirement on borrowing is definite but the revenue generation is not guaranteed.' If savings do not materialise, the revenue budget faces a direct impact from unrecovered borrowing costs.
findings.matters: A shortfall in projected revenue savings converts these into unrecovered borrowing costs, directly increasing the net revenue cost and reducing resources available for debt service.
findings.figures: Invest to Save schemes: £15m; Property Acquisition Programme (net borrowing): £10.452m; In-House Residential Provision: £2.5m
findings.quote: If these costs were removed from the figures in Table 1, it would reduce the overall percentage figure. However, for prudence the figures are included on the basis that the requirement on borrowing is definite but the revenue generation is not guaranteed.

findings.paper_title: Final Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2028-29 v3 Cabinet briefing
findings.headline: BCIL funding shortfall of £0.914m will require additional borrowing or programme cuts
findings.detail: The council's Community Infrastructure Levy funding commitments (£15.305m) exceed available BCIL (£14.391m) by £0.914m. This gap has arisen due to downward CIL projections and remains unresolved. The document states the shortfall 'will be regularly monitored' but notes that 'if this could not be mitigated, the funding source of these projects would need to be reverted to borrowing,' increasing capital financing costs and revenue budget impact.
findings.matters: An unplanned £0.914m borrowing requirement increases the council's debt burden beyond current MTFS assumptions, further reducing debt service capacity.
findings.figures: BCIL available: £14.391m; BCIL requirements: £15.305m; shortfall: £0.914m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Harrow is funding a £1.25m Regeneration Team through capital receipts flexibility in 2026/27
findings.detail: The 2026/27 MTFS includes a budget of £1.250m for the Regeneration Team, which the council will fund through capital receipts flexibility rather than from core revenue budget. The cost will be removed from the budget and funded by capital receipts instead. However, the MTFS does not assume any further use of capital receipts flexibility from 2027/28 onwards, meaning this is a one-year funding measure.
findings.matters: For lenders, this signals that the council is using a temporary flexibility to fund what will become an ongoing revenue cost. The question of how the team will be funded from 2027/28 onwards is important for assessing budget sustainability and whether the council's core revenue position can support this activity.
findings.quote: The 2026/27 MTFS includes a budget of £1.250m to fund the Regeneration Team.  The nature of this spend meets the capital flexibility criteria and the team will be funded under the capital flexibilities scheme.

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: Right-to-Buy receipt utilisation must complete within timescales; sales volumes are currently low and plan assumes 6 disposals in 2026/27, risking under-deployment and clawback to government.
findings.detail: The Council retains 100% of RTB receipts (new policy from 2026/27). The 30-year plan assumes full utilisation of £105.721m RTB receipts over 30 years, with zero clawback. However, the paper notes 'Sales volumes remain low' and assumes only 6 disposals in 2026/27 and 'thereafter' (implying 6 per year thereafter). Any failure to deploy receipts within the required timescales (currently 3 years) results in repayment to government plus interest penalties.
findings.matters: RTB receipts are a key financing source for new build. If volumes fall short of plan or deployment is delayed, the Council loses this funding and must compensate from borrowing or reserves. The plan assumes £2.240m receipts in year 1, but if this does not materialise, it creates a £2m+ funding gap. This has proven difficult to forecast (the recent 'spike' in applications ahead of November 2024 discount change confirms volatility).
findings.figures: Total RTB receipts assumed £105.721m over 30 years; 6 disposals assumed in 2026/27; average valuation £423k, average discount £16k (based on new government policy from November 2024); receipt utilisation timeline 3 years
findings.quote: Sales volumes remain low, but there was a spike in applications ahead of the November 2024 discount change.

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: Awaab's Law compliance requirements are now live (27 October 2025); budget set but Council notes further tightening of standards may increase costs, flagged AMBER risk.
findings.detail: The Hazards in Social Housing (Prescribed Requirements) (England) Regulations 2025 (Awaab's Law) came into force 27 October 2025, requiring social landlords to address emergency hazards and damp/mould hazards within fixed timescales. The Council has budgeted for this and increased compliance work ('increased focus in areas such as asbestos, electrical safety and water hygiene with new 5-year contracts put in place in March 2024'). However, the risk register explicitly flags 'Additional costs incurred because of tightened or increased compliance workloads' as AMBER, with note that standards/timescales may tighten further.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law creates a statutory duty with financial penalties for breach. If inspection and remediation timescales are tightened beyond current assumptions (e.g., from 3 months to 30 days for damp/mould), or if prevalence of non-compliance is higher than budgeted, costs could spike. This is a new regulatory burden with limited track record of actual costs.
findings.figures: Budget provision included; EICR (electrical inspections) moving to 5-year cycles; bi-annual fire door checks noted as 'likely need'
findings.quote: The Hazards in Social Housing (Prescribed Requirements) (England) Regulations 2025, commonly referred to as Awaab's Law, came into force for the social housing sector on 27 October 2025. Social landlords are now required to address all emergency hazards and all damp and mould hazards that present a significant risk of harm to tenants to fixed timeframes.

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: Service charge increases for general needs tenants (8.16%) exceed CPI, indicating actual cost pressures; general affordability concerns raised in resident consultation.
findings.detail: Service charges for general needs are increasing by 8.16% (from £9.40 to £10.17 per week), well above the assumed CPI increase of 3.8%. The paper states charges 'are updated to reflect inflation and actual usage or costs incurred in the year' and bases them on '100% cost recovery'. This suggests cost inflation in communal services. Separately, the consultation noted only 72 residents responded, but many raised concerns about rent affordability; the Council is also increasing rents by 4.8% plus rent convergence (£1–2/week additional from 2027/28).
findings.matters: If service costs are rising faster than CPI, it signals underlying cost pressures in estate management, utilities, or maintenance that are not being offset by operational efficiencies. Combined with 4.8% rent rises, tenants face double-digit total increases in some cases. This risks increased arrears (flagged AMBER in risk register as 'Tenants cannot afford increases') and bad debt, which is already assumed at 0.69% of rent.
findings.figures: Service charge increase 8.16% (vs. 3.8% CPI); rent increase 4.8%; rent convergence adds £1/week (2027/28) and £2/week (2028/29) for eligible tenants; 72 residents consulted
findings.quote: Approve proposed average weekly service charge for general needs tenants of £9.40 for 2026/27, representing an average increase of 8.16% from 2025/26

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: Interest rate assumptions for borrowing may be optimistic; the plan assumes rates fall to 4.58% in 2027/28 before rising to 5.05%, and flagged as AMBER risk.
findings.detail: The 10-year business plan assumes new borrowing at 4.85% (2026/27), 4.58% (2027/28), 5.05% (thereafter). These are based on February 2026 Treasury Management Report forecasts. Current average HRA borrowing rate is 4.42%, and £301m new borrowing is forecast over 10 years. If rates remain above 4.85% or fall less steeply than assumed, interest costs will exceed plan — the risk register explicitly flags 'Interest rates – rise above plan' as AMBER.
findings.matters: Every 0.1% increase in average borrowing cost = £301m × 0.001 = £301k additional annual cost by year 10. Interest payable in 2026/27 is £9.113m; if rates are higher than assumed and borrowing reaches £301m cumulative, interest costs could reach £15m+. This directly impacts HRA affordability and headroom in reserves.
findings.figures: New borrowing assumed at 4.85% (2026/27), 4.58% (2027/28), 5.05% (thereafter); total new borrowing £301m over 10 years; current average rate 4.42%; interest payable 2026/27 £9.113m
findings.quote: For planning purposes, interest on new borrowing is assumed at 4.85% in 2026/27, reducing to 4.58% in 2027/28 and 5.05% thereafter.

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: The capital programme depends critically on grant funding and new build delivery; any delay to major schemes risks grant clawback and rental income assumptions.
findings.detail: £572.045m of the £751.419m capital programme is for new affordable homes (1,100 homes by 2036). Financing is £274.887m grants (37%), £300.889m borrowing (40%), the remainder from capital receipts and reserves. Three major schemes are on the critical path: Byron Quarter (planning consent December 2025, site start March 2026, 2-year build), Poets Corner Phase 1 (530 homes, planning status unclear), and Grange Farm Phase 2A (45 homes, approved February 2025). The AMBER risk register flags 'Delays to starts on site and completions risk grant drawdown and rental income'.
findings.matters: New homes are central to the business plan's revenue growth assumptions. If Byron Quarter or Poets Corner are delayed, the Council loses both grant funding (which has conditions on drawdown timescales) and the rental income that is forecast from 2027/28 onwards. The 10-year business plan shows net rent income growing from £43.2m to £73.0m (a 69% increase), heavily dependent on completion of new stock.
findings.figures: £572.045m new homes programme; £274.887m grants; Byron Quarter 149 homes starting March 2026; Grange Farm Phase 2A 45 homes approved; Poets Corner up to 1,058 homes
findings.quote: Planning consent was granted in December 2025, and following discharge of conditions, contracts are expected to be finalised early 2026 ahead of a start on site by March 2026. Construction is expected to take two years.

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: HRA reserves are being drawn down by £7.3m in the first year — a 56% reduction — to fund capital investment despite operating surpluses.
findings.detail: General balances fall from £13.031m (31 March 2025) to £5.693m (31 March 2026), remaining above the 7% minimum requirement (£3.025m) but representing a significant reduction in headroom. The drawdown is to fund capital investment: the operating account shows a £2.023m deficit covered by £9.361m revenue contribution to capital outlay. Over the MTFS period, reserves stabilise around £5.5m but remain tight relative to capital ambitions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's cash position is being depleted to fund investment that may not generate sufficient rental income, or whether there is structural deficit emerging. The tightness of reserves limits flexibility for unexpected costs or delays to new build revenue streams.
findings.figures: Reserves fall from £13.031m to £5.693m (year 1), £5.020m (year 2), £5.498m (year 3); minimum required £3.025m–£3.453m
findings.quote: HRA Balance Brought Forward (13,031) [£'000] … HRA Balance Carried Forward (5,693) [£'000]

findings.paper_title: 20267 HRA Budget and refreshed 30-year Business Plan
findings.headline: Disrepair claims have become a material cost pressure, with an additional £489k provision for legal costs and compensation based on trend analysis.
findings.detail: The Council has increased the disrepair budget by £489k beyond base provision, citing 'increased demand in the sector' and revised estimates based on prior years' trends. This is compensations and legal costs, not one-off items. The AMBER risk register flags this as potentially tightening further if compliance standards change.
findings.matters: Disrepair claims are compensations for breach of implied warranty of fitness — they represent a liability for past failures. An upward trend across the sector suggests either increasing enforcement activity or deteriorating stock condition. This cost is difficult to control and represents risk of further deterioration.
findings.figures: £489k additional provision; flagged as trend-based from 'previous years' disrepair cases'
findings.quote: There is increased demand in the sector on disrepair cases and as such there is an additional £489k to cover anticipated legal costs and compensations based on revised budget estimates from the trend of previous years' disrepair cases.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget 2026-27 and MTFS Report -19 Feb 2026 - FINAL version 2026-02-10 (clear copy for the Leader)
findings.headline: Children's services faces £6.5m pressure in 2025-26, driven by placement costs and staff costs
findings.detail: Despite being a statutory service, Children's Services is showing a £6.5m cost pressure, with £3.7m relating to placement costs and the remainder to staff costs. The council is exploring alternative accommodation solutions to reduce placement costs and reviewing agency staff use.
findings.matters: Placement costs and staffing are both difficult to reduce in child protection services. If savings plans do not materialise, this recurring pressure will continue to draw on central contingencies.
findings.figures: £6.5m total pressure; £3.7m placements; remainder staff costs
findings.quote: Children's Services – there is a forecast pressure of £6.5m, with £3.7m of this relating to cost pressures on placements and the rest relating to staff costs. Alternative accommodation, e.g. semi-independent living, is being explored to reduce placement costs. The use of agency staff will also be reviewed to reduce spend.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget 2026-27 and MTFS Report -19 Feb 2026 - FINAL version 2026-02-10 (clear copy for the Leader)
findings.headline: Budget Planning Reserve and general fund balances (£32.8m combined) are fully committed to cover DSG deficit; minimal contingency buffer remains
findings.detail: Total general fund reserves are £49m, but the forecast DSG deficit of £32.1m is just under the combined total of the Budget Planning Reserve (£22.8m) and general fund balances (£10m). This means the two primary tools for managing unforeseen risks are already earmarked to cover a known liability, leaving minimal discretionary buffer.
findings.matters: Reserves that appear adequate in absolute terms are actually spoken for by a single contingent liability. Any additional pressures (demand spikes, cost inflation, funding shortfalls) cannot easily be absorbed without triggering further deficit budgeting.
findings.figures: Budget Planning Reserve £22.8m; General Fund Balances £10m; DSG deficit £32.1m
findings.quote: There is a forecast DSG deficit of £32.1m which is a significant sum and is just under the combined total of £32.8m for the Budget Planning reserve (£22.8m) and the General fund balances (£10.m)

findings.paper_title: Final Budget 2026-27 and MTFS Report -19 Feb 2026 - FINAL version 2026-02-10 (clear copy for the Leader)
findings.headline: Council tax base declined by 214 Band D properties between 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.detail: The tax base fell from 90,843 to 90,629 Band D equivalent properties, a reduction caused primarily by lower-than-anticipated Council Tax premiums (surcharges on second homes). This reduced 2026-27 council tax income by £678k. Council tax comprises 80% of the council's net revenue budget.
findings.matters: A declining tax base erodes the primary funding source at a time when the council is heavily dependent on it. Further base decline would worsen budget pressures, particularly in 2027-28 and 2028-29.
findings.figures: 214 property reduction; £678k lost income 2026-27; 80% of budget from council tax
findings.quote: The tax base of 90,629 compares with a tax base of 90,843 set for the financial year 2025/26. This is a decrease of 214 Band D equivalent properties and has arisen predominantly due to the volumes of Council Tax premiums payable being lower than had previously been anticipated.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget 2026-27 and MTFS Report -19 Feb 2026 - FINAL version 2026-02-10 (clear copy for the Leader)
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review leaves Harrow £0.3m worse off over 3 years; only 10 of 20 outer London boroughs gain grant
findings.detail: Initial modelling showed Harrow would lose £4m in grant from the Fair Funding Review's new allocation methodology. Although government's additional £3.4bn national allocation reduced the impact to a net loss of £0.3m over 3 years, Harrow remains one of only 10 outer London boroughs to lose grant, and was one of 149 councils on the shared moderngov.co.uk platform (not on own host).
findings.matters: The council's financial recovery plan assumes stable or improving grant funding. A net loss of grant, combined with 80% reliance on council tax, indicates limited room to improve funding position without further council tax rises.
findings.figures: £0.3m net 3-year loss; initial model showed £4m loss
findings.quote: The initial figures provided on an Authority-by-Authority basis set out that despite being an outer London Borough, Harrow would lose grant of £4m over three years. In fact, of 20 Outer London Boroughs, only 10 Outer London Boroughs are estimated to gain grant on a like for like basis when compared to the 2025/26 baseline.

findings.paper_title: Final Budget 2026-27 and MTFS Report -19 Feb 2026 - FINAL version 2026-02-10 (clear copy for the Leader)
findings.headline: Emissions Trading Scheme liability of £2.88m forecast for 2028-29 from waste disposal authority is an unforeseen cost
findings.detail: The West London Waste Authority's budget report estimates £20m collective ETS liability across the 6 boroughs it serves, based on fossil carbon content of residual waste being charged at £98/tonne. Harrow's apportioned share is estimated at £2.88m in 2028-29. This is a new, unanticipated obligation that was not factored into the MTFS until discovered in January 2026.

findings.paper_title: 12F) TMSS - Appendix F
findings.headline: HRA new-build housing schemes are increasingly unable to demonstrate positive financial returns, requiring subsidy to enable delivery.
findings.detail: The Council requires all new Housing Revenue Account developments to achieve positive Net Present Value (NPV) for long-term sustainability. However, the strategy explicitly states this requirement is 'increasingly challenging to deliver' due to the Council's zero-carbon building commitment and construction cost inflation. To enable housing delivery, the Council has created an exception process allowing negative-NPV schemes if they provide clear environmental or social impact—effectively requiring General Fund subsidy.
findings.matters: Housing development unable to achieve positive returns signals either unsustainable market economics or structural need for subsidy. This impacts both HRA financial sustainability and the council's regeneration capacity. The 30-year HRA business plan undergoes fundamental refresh this year (adoption February 2026), which may reflect revised assumptions about housing viability.
findings.figures: Current HRA Loan-to-Value ratio 49% (below 70% maximum threshold); minimum working balance requirement 7% of rental and service charges income
findings.quote: This requirement is becoming increasingly challenging to deliver given the high demand for social housing, the Council's commitment to delivering zero-carbon compliant homes, and wider construction-related inflationary pressures.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs are rising steeply, growing from 11.98% to 13.58% of the revenue budget between 2026/27 and 2028/29.

These costs are already factored into the medium-term financial strategy but represent an accelerating trend that progressively constrains revenue budget flexibility for service delivery.
findings.matters: Rising capital financing costs reduce financial flexibility to respond to service pressures and economic shocks. A lender needs to understand whether this debt service trajectory is sustainable and whether the council can maintain service delivery while servicing debt at this level.

findings.paper_title: 8B) Harrow Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25 (03.02.26)
findings.headline: Fund investment returned 3.1%, falling 2.3 percentage points short of its 5.5% benchmark
findings.detail: The Fund underperformed its benchmark materially over the year. The shortfall is attributed partly to active equity managers underweighting stocks that drove much of the market's gain, but 2.3% annual underperformance signals either strategy misalignment or manager performance issues. Given that investment returns fund future liabilities, this drag matters.
findings.matters: Consistent underperformance increases the council's contribution burden and delays recovery of the fund deficit. Benchmark misses also raise questions about manager selection and monitoring.
findings.figures: Return 3.1%, benchmark 5.5%, shortfall 2.3 percentage points
findings.quote: The Fund's overall investment return for the year was 3.1%, which was 2.3% below its benchmark return of 5.5%.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8B) Harrow Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25 (03.02.26)
findings.headline: Pension administration hitting multiple performance targets badly—cases are routinely delayed
findings.detail: The Fund is not meeting statutory performance standards for basic pension administration. Dependent benefit notifications achieved only 36.36% of cases within 5 days; deferred benefit calculations hit just 48.69% of the 10-day target; refund processing is 68.06% within 5 days. The paper lists nine key metrics; six are below 75% achievement. No explanation is offered for why these critical times are being missed.
findings.matters: Poor pension administration creates legal and reputational risk, suggests possible staffing or system constraints, and indicates the council is not managing member communication effectively. This reflects on the council's operational capability.
findings.figures: Dependent benefit notifications 36.36% of target; deferred benefits 48.69%; retirement benefit estimate 64.94%; transfer statutory notification 58.82%; refund processing 68.06%
findings.quote: Calculation and notification of deferred benefits 10 days 48.69%

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8C) Audit Completion Report 050226 Final
findings.headline: Prior year fraud allegations (August 2021) remain under investigation with control recommendations still being implemented
findings.detail: In August 2021, the Council received allegations of fraud and corruption currently subject to police criminal investigation. Internal audit found only 'limited assurance' over controls in the affected department in 2024, citing lack of supporting documentation and high staff turnover preventing recommendations being addressed. The Council formed an action plan with 16 high and medium rated recommendations. At end of 2024/25, one high-rated and four medium-rated recommendations remain unimplemented.
findings.matters: Serious fraud allegations from 2021 remain unresolved nearly four years later, with recommendations still being implemented. Continued limited assurance over controls in the affected department suggests underlying governance and compliance weaknesses have not been adequately addressed.
findings.figures: Allegations made August 2021; still under criminal investigation in 2025; 16 recommendations in response plan; 5 still unimplemented at year-end 2024/25
findings.quote: In August 2021, the Council were alerted to allegations of fraud and corruption that are currently subject to a criminal investigation by the Police... Internal audit undertook a further review during 2024, with the report being issued in December 2024. This review concluded that there was a limited level of assurance in the controls in place... At the end of 2024/25, one high rated and four medium rated recommendations were yet to be implemented.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8C) Audit Completion Report 050226 Final
findings.headline: Schools PFI contract unmonitored since 2021/22; internal audit found no assurance in controls; 14 recommendations outstanding
findings.detail: Internal audit completed review of the schools PFI contract and issued 'No assurance' opinion on control effectiveness. The contracts team was disbanded in 2021/22 restructure with no handover process. Almost all staff with knowledge of the PFI have left. The contract has gone unmonitored for years. Internal audit raised 14 recommendations (12 high risk, 2 medium risk) to address control weaknesses. The Council's action plan to implement improvements is scheduled for 2025/26 and not yet executed.
findings.matters: An unmonitored PFI contract creates risk of overpayment for services not received, hidden liabilities, and unknown commitments. Years of non-monitoring indicates a serious control breakdown in contract governance.
findings.figures: 14 recommendations (12 high risk, 2 medium); contract unmonitored since 2021/22 (approximately 3+ years); all remedial actions scheduled for 2025/26
findings.quote: the schools PFI contract had not been monitored, and no handover process had been put in place at the time of the restructure. While this was raised with Senior Management in the Place department in 2022, it was not addressed and almost all staff with knowledge of the schools PFI have left the Council, with limited knowledge retained. The internal audit report raised 14 recommendations for the Council to address the weaknesses identified, 12 of which were categorised as High risk and the other 2 as Medium risk.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8C) Audit Completion Report 050226 Final
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has spiralled from £1.8m to £13.8m with £28m projected by end of 2025/26
findings.detail: The DSG reserve deficit opened at £1.8m and ballooned to £13.8m by year-end 2024/25, driven by £13.7m overspend on the High Needs Block (EHCP placements). Q1 2025/26 projections show the cumulative deficit reaching £28m, a £14.1m overspend in a single year. The recovery plan's critical first milestone was a new special school (292 places, 30% reduction in independent placements, £2.5m annual savings), but DfE approval has been delayed with increased uncertainty it will proceed. The Council holds only £10m in general fund reserves against a projected £28m DSG deficit.
findings.matters: The council faces an uncontrolled, ring-fenced deficit spiralling out of control. The primary recovery strategy (new special school) is stalled. With only £10m general reserves against a £28m projected deficit, the council lacks financial resources to manage this escalating demand.
findings.figures: Opening DSG deficit £1.8m; current deficit £13.8m; projected 2025/26 deficit £28m; new school projected to deliver £2.5m annual savings; council general fund reserves £10m; High Needs overspend £13.7m in one year
findings.quote: The Council had an opening Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) reserve deficit of £1.8m, but this deficit increased to £13.8m by the end of 2024/25... The Council's Budget Monitoring Report for Q1 of 2025/26, taken to Cabinet in September 2025, projected the cumulative deficit at the end of 2025/26 to be £28m... However, senior officers at the Council have stated that the DfE have pushed this decision back, and there is increased uncertainty as to whether final approval for the school will be granted.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8C) Audit Completion Report 050226 Final
findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimed opinion: no assurance over council's financial statements
findings.detail: The auditors cannot express an opinion on whether financial statements are true and fair. This follows a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24. Due to backstop legislation and time constraints, the Council cannot complete sufficient procedures to rebuild assurance over opening balances by the 27 February 2026 publication deadline. The auditors plan to work on rebuilding assurance in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the financial statements are not independently verified as reliable. Lenders cannot rely on the accounts as presented or make lending decisions based on the published figures.
findings.figures: Backstop publication date 27 February 2026; two consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2023/24 and 2024/25)
findings.quote: it has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion. For this reason, we will be issuing a disclaimed opinion in time for the Council to publish its financial statements by the backstop date of 27 February 2026

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8D) Audit Completion Report Pension Fund 040226
findings.headline: Creditor control account reconciliations remain performed late with variances unresolved, a control deficiency repeated from prior audit
findings.detail: This weakness was identified in prior year audits and remains unfixed in 2024/25. The Council reconciles payables and ledger modules more than a month after month-end, leaving identified discrepancies unresolved. The auditors' 2024/25 walkthrough found the same pattern: discrepancies were again left as 'reconciling differences' without investigation, despite management committing to fix the process.
findings.matters: Late reconciliations with unresolved variances indicate weak financial controls and increase risk of inaccurate creditor records. The audit notes this could result in invoices being paid outside agreed terms and unnecessary interest costs.
findings.figures: Reconciliations performed over one month after month-end; specific variance amounts not disclosed
findings.quote: Our walkthroughs of the creditors system in 2024/25 identified discrepancies which again were left as reconciling differences. Our recommendation below remains open.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee
findings.paper_title: 8D) Audit Completion Report Pension Fund 040226
findings.headline: £1.326 million unadjusted misstatement identified between pension fund investment valuations in accounts and external fund manager confirmations
findings.detail: Auditors tested 100% of the £135 million level 3 fair value hierarchy investments and identified a £1.326 million difference between valuations recorded in the financial statements and external confirmations from fund managers. This variance was not adjusted by management, despite being unadjusted misstatement of sufficient size to report to the audit committee.
findings.matters: A £1.326 million variance in investment valuations signals potential control weaknesses in how the pension fund reconciles investment confirmations, which indicates risk in the council's financial recording systems.
findings.figures: £1.326 million; £135 million total level 3 investments tested
findings.quote: We have identified an unadjusted misstatement of £1.326 million, which relates to differences between the valuation of investments disclosed in the financial statements and external confirmations provided by fund managers.

news_drafts.headline: Harrow faces £3m overspend as temporary accommodation and children's care costs surge
news_drafts.lead: Harrow Council is forecasting a net overspend of £3.039m for the current financial year after planned use of reserves, according to figures presented to cabinet on Wednesday. The shortfall is driven by two structural pressures: temporary accommodation for homeless households, which is costing the council £15.7m a year more than government subsidy covers, and children's services placements, where 25 children in residential homes at an average £7,000 per week are creating a £7.249m overspend. The council has approved a savings programme of £4.062m for the year, but nearly half of those savings depend on completing capital projects—acquiring 50 new homes for temporary housing, selling properties at Sheldon House, and investing in residential care provision—that are rated as at-risk and may not deliver on schedule.

news_drafts.headline: Harrow Council forecasts £3m overspend on day-to-day spending for current year
news_drafts.lead: Harrow Council's Cabinet was told on Thursday that the authority is forecasting a net overspend of £3.039m on its revenue spending (day-to-day running costs) for 2026-27, which would consume its budget planning reserves if not contained by year-end. The largest single pressure is temporary accommodation for homeless households, where demand has tripled in three years to 726 households, creating a £15.7m annual subsidy loss as government funding falls short of market costs. Children's services is overspending by £7.2m, driven chiefly by residential placements at average costs of £7,000 per week, while schools-related funding has a £54.2m accumulated deficit that grows by £24.6m this year. The council is relying on government support to cover 90 per cent of that deficit, though approval of its special educational needs reform plan remains conditional. The Cabinet also approved a savings programme of £4.062m, but nearly half depends on capital projects succeeding.
